record.context_brief: Matching rules with perimeter discrepancy bounds
record.original_question: Find local matching rules for quasicrystal tilings in dimension 2 or 3 such that both of the following hold. First, for every tile type t and every finite region R made of tiles, the discrepancy D_t(R)=|N_t(R)-d(t)vol(R)| is bounded by c_t |∂R| for some constant c_t depending only on t, where N_t(R) counts tiles of type t in R and d(t) is the density of t. Second, the same perimeter-order discrepancy bound holds for every pattern or patch that satisfies the matching rules.

evidence.quote: (A) Given a tile t and a region R of the tiling space made of a finite union of tiles, define the discrepancy Dt (R) of the tile t in R as Dt (R) := |Nt (R) − d(t) · vol(R)|. Here, Nt (R) stands for the cardinality of the number of tiles t in the region R and d(t) for the density of the tile t. The first condition imposed on the tiling is that of 'low fluctuation'; that is, that there exists a constant ct depending only on the tile t such that Dt (R) ≤ ct · |∂R|.

(B) The second condition is that property (A) should also hold for any pattern or patch satisfying the given matching rule. Problem 2.7.3. Find a set of matching rules in dimension 2 and/or 3 that meet both condition (A) and condition (B).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider tilings of $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d\in\{2,3\}$ built from a finite set $\mathcal{T}$ of prototiles (closed sets, each a polytope or a translate of a fixed shape, considered up to a fixed group of allowed motions). A local matching rule is a finite set of allowed configurations: a tiling $\mathcal{T}\text{-tiling}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfies the rule if every patch of bounded radius around each tile belongs to the allowed list. Assume every tiling satisfying the rule is repetitive and has, for each prototile $t\in\mathcal{T}$, a well-defined frequency (density) $d(t)>0$.

For a tile type $t\in\mathcal{T}$ and a finite region $R$ that is a finite union of tiles of the tiling, let $N_t(R)$ denote the number of tiles of type $t$ contained in $R$, let $\mathrm{vol}(R)$ denote its $d$-dimensional volume, and let $|\partial R|$ denote the $(d-1)$-dimensional measure of its boundary. Define the discrepancy
$$D_t(R)\;:=\;\bigl|N_t(R)-d(t)\,\mathrm{vol}(R)\bigr|.$$

Problem. Construct, in dimension $d=2$ and/or $d=3$, an explicit set of local matching rules together with a tiling space such that both of the following hold.

(A) (Low fluctuation of the tiling.) For every prototile $t\in\mathcal{T}$ there exists a constant $c_t>0$, depending only on $t$, such that for every finite region $R$ which is a union of tiles,
$$D_t(R)\;\le\;c_t\,|\partial R|.$$

(B) (Stability under the matching rule.) The same perimeter-order discrepancy bound in (A) holds for every tiling, pattern, or patch that satisfies the given matching rule (not only for a single distinguished tiling).
artifact.status_search_result: General context exists: weak matching rules are known to bound perp-space fluctuations for many N-fold symmetric tilings, and matching rules for 3D Penrose tilings exist. However, no source found directly resolves the specific requirement that a perimeter-order bound D_t(R) ≤ c_t|∂R| hold both for a tiling and for every patch obeying the matching rule in dimensions 2 or 3. Status appears unknown from available sources.

status_evidence.title: Weak matching rules for quasicrystals
status_evidence.snippet: Weak matching rules ... ensure that fluctuations in perp-space are uniformly bounded. They exist for N-fold symmetric tilings when N is not divisible by four.
status_evidence.claim: Weak matching rules controlling fluctuations are known to exist for many quasicrystal tilings, but the specific perimeter-order discrepancy formulation is not directly addressed.

status_evidence.title: Theory of Matching Rules for the 3-Dimensional Penrose Tilings
status_evidence.snippet: Matching rules for 3-dimensional Penrose tilings exist as local alternatives to global projection methods.
status_evidence.claim: 3D matching rules exist, but the discrepancy/stability conditions (A)+(B) are not shown.
